Related posts are a common feature on CMSes like blogs, using simple text comparison. When you are viewing a post about cats, it can show a list of 5 most relevant cat posts in the sidebar.

Pros:

  • It can encourage people to dig further into a subject. If you are reading the news on X and there were other articles about X recently, you can go read those too.

  • It can reveal how common a topic is, or even expose reposts (like if all 5 related posts were the same title as the post you are on)

  • It can promote smaller subs and alternative viewpoints. If you are reading a post in a big generic sub, e.g. a link in /v/news about the Silk Road developer, there could be a related post in /v/silkroad (doesn’t exist, just an example) with more in-depth discussion because people on niche subs tend to have specialised knowledge.

Cons:

  • Full text comparison is computationally expensive on large databases. You could compromise on the accuracy of “relatedness” by only comparing titles or partial post content.

As a temporary measure, and something useful to know anyway:

Middle-click, Ctrl-click (on Windows), or Cmd-click (on OS X) should open most links in a new tab.

From a previous suggestion. I use middle-click if I want to open in a new tab, instead of relying on a site-specific feature. This way I have a choice to open in the same tab by left-clicking.

If you use Greasemonkey for Firefox, here's a script that does just that. Also makes links open in a new window when not logged in. Also opens user profiles ("a.author") and links to subs ("a.subverse") in a new window. Sub links in the title bar are left untouched...

// ==UserScript==
// \@name voat
// \@namespace voat
// \@description voat
// \@include \https://voat.co/*
// \@version 1
// \@grant none
// ==/UserScript==


document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function(event) {
 Array.filter(document.querySelectorAll("a.title, a.comments, a.author, a.subverse"), function(element){
 element.target = "_blank";
 });
});
